before.rope_note: Class 2 walk-up on the SW slopes; no rope or technical protection used on this specific line (other Cloudy Peak approaches have 3rd/4th class sections, but the SW Slopes route itself is non-technical).

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long day regardless of approach - Cloudy Pass alone is roughly 22 miles round trip with about 4,700 ft of gain from the Phelps Creek trailhead via Spider Meadow and Spider Gap, before the summit scramble even starts; partner should be fit for a full 10-14 hour day, or plan to backpack in and use Lyman Lakes/Cloudy Pass as a base camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light daypack if summiting from a Lyman Lakes/Cloudy Pass camp; full overnight pack (30-40 lb) if doing the approach and summit car-to-car with gear

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - roughly 11 miles one-way from the Phelps Creek trailhead to Cloudy Pass (about 22 miles round trip); most parties backpack in rather than attempt it as a single push
requiredSkills: off-trail route-finding on open heather and talus slopes
early-season snow travel awareness if attempting before the route is fully melted out
basic wilderness navigation - no maintained trail to the summit
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable on unmaintained, off-trail Class 2 terrain; prior scrambling experience helpful given the loose scree hazard, but no technical climbing background required

weather.typical: Transitional Cascades climate - generally stable and dry in the July-September window, with spring/early-season snow cover on the slopes being the main lingering hazard
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible over exposed Cascade ridgelines in summer

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low-to-moderate; sustained Class 2 heather and talus with the loose scree hazard being the main slip/fall concern, worse when snow lingers early season - terrain is not sustained cliff-exposed

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble; also outside NWAC's mapped forecast zones (Cloudy Peak sits east of the Cascade crest in the Entiat Mountains/eastern Glacier Peak Wilderness, which NWAC does not directly cover)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; the route climbs open heather and talus directly from Cloudy Pass to the summit, not the nearby Spider Glacier/snowfield

itinerary.cal: Glacier Peak Wilderness requires a free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead; the Holden Village approach needs a Lady of the Lake ferry reservation, while the longer, ferry-free alternative is via the Trinity trailhead over Spider Gap (glacier travel, more gain, not needed just for this peak).

days.note: Most parties reach Cloudy Peak via Holden Village (Lady of the Lake ferry across Lake Chelan, then bus to the village) and hike the Railroad Creek / Hart-Lyman Lake trail up the valley. It's a long but gentle, well-graded trail past Hart Lake and Crown Point Falls to Lyman Lake, with Cloudy Pass just beyond — camp at Lyman Lake or up at the pass itself.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach Lyman Lake / Cloudy Pass camp

days.note: Leave camp with a light pack and climb from Cloudy Pass up open slopes to gain the southwest ridge, then follow the ridge to the summit block. The final moves are class 3-4 on the block itself — most parties traverse to its north side to find the easiest weakness, and some choose to belay the last few moves.

waypoints.name: Phelps Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trail #1511 starts on an old mining road; self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Coles Corner take WA-207 north, then Chiwawa River Road (FR-62) about 22 miles — paved for the first eleven, gravel and rough after that — and finish with 2.3 miles up Phelps Creek Road (FR-6211) to the road end. Low-clearance vehicles struggle on the last stretch. Cloudy Pass can also be reached from Holden Village up Railroad Creek or from Trinity over Buck Creek Pass, but both are longer multi-day alternatives; the waypoints below follow the Phelps Creek line.

waypoints.name: Leroy Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Largest of roughly 16 creek crossings on the approach and often the wettest ford; an unmaintained climbers' path branches here toward Leroy Basin.
waypoints.directions: Follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the valley on an old mining grade, crossing into the Glacier Peak Wilderness around the two-and-a-half-mile mark. The grade is gentle and Phelps Creek runs alongside the whole way, so water is never a concern. Leroy Creek is the largest of the tributary crossings and the one most likely to soak your feet; the unmaintained path climbing toward Leroy Basin leaves here and is not your turn.

waypoints.name: Spider Meadow
waypoints.note: Broad subalpine meadow with established camps at its upper end; no campfires allowed (prohibited above 4,000 ft).
waypoints.directions: Stay on #1511 as the valley opens out — roughly 1,900 ft of gain over the six and a half miles from the car, so this is easy ground. The meadow is the last flat, sheltered camping before the climb to the gap, and it is the obvious place to stage from if you are not going car-to-car.

waypoints.name: Spider Gap / Spider Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, cairned route climbs steep loose scree then crosses a permanent snowfield (the shrinking Spider Glacier) to the gap; microspikes and an ice axe are recommended even in summer.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow the trail climbs into upper Phelps Basin and the maintained tread gives out; a cairned, unmaintained line goes up steep loose scree to the base of the snow around 5,300 ft. From there about half a mile of permanent snowfield leads to the gap. It generally boots or plunge-steps easily in summer, but early season brings open crevasses and firm refrozen snow, and a whiteout or a morning refreeze turns the axe and traction from optional into necessary.

waypoints.name: Cloudy Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow saddle above the Lyman Lakes basin where the climbers' trail toward Cloudy Peak's southwest ridge leaves the maintained Cloudy Pass Trail #1256.
waypoints.directions: Descend the north side of the gap. The first hundred vertical feet are the steepest, with the softer, less sun-affected snow usually on the climber's-left (north) side, and it eases into scree and then a gentler snowfield. Follow the basin down past the Lyman Glacier and the Upper Lyman Lakes to Lower Lyman Lake, then climb back up through open meadows to the pass — several miles for a modest net loss and regain, and the pass is the normal camp for the peak.

waypoints.name: Southwest ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Climbers' path through meadows fades into heather benches and then talus; aim for the broad crest of the southwest ridge above the pass.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and head roughly north-northeast up open wildflower meadows on an obvious boot path. The path fades onto heather benches and then talus; keep working toward the broad crest of the southwest ridge rather than contouring across the slopes below it.

waypoints.name: Notch below the summit block
waypoints.note: A notch separates the ridge from the summit block, blocking the direct line; traverse climber's-right around to the north side of the block to find the scramble route (helmet recommended - falls here would be serious).
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest of the ridge itself. Straying onto the flanking slopes drops you into seriously unstable scree that is both slower and harder to reverse, and the crest falls away sharply on its far (north) side. Pick a deliberate line through the loose talus blocks — this is exactly the terrain for knocking rock onto a partner, so spread out and keep helmets on.

waypoints.name: Cloudy Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained by a short, exposed Class 3-4 scramble on the north side of the block; first climbed in 1921 by a Mountaineers party.
waypoints.directions: The notch blocks the direct line, so traverse climber's-right around the east side of the summit block and keep going onto its north (back) side, where a short Class 3-4 weakness leads to the top. It is narrow with real exposure and is the technical crux of the route; cautious parties rope the last few moves.

before.approach: The standard approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft), at the end of Forest Road 6211 off the Chiwawa River Road (FR 62) north of Leavenworth. From the trailhead, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the valley along Phelps Creek, gaining about 1,900 ft over 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows; you enter the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary around the 2.5-mile mark, and Phelps Creek itself is the reliable water source the whole way up (a couple of minor tributary crossings, easy on foot/log in normal summer flow). Beyond the meadows the trail climbs into upper Phelps Basin toward the base of Spider Glacier at roughly 5,300 ft, then ascends the glacier/snowfield about 0.5 mile to Spider Gap (7,100 ft) — this is the crux of the approach: it's a permanent snow/glacier slope that is generally a straightforward boot-pack or plunge-step in summer but can have open crevasses and firm, icy conditions early season, so carry (and know how to use) an ice axe, and microspikes are a common recommendation; whiteout or early-morning refreeze can make an axe/crampons more than optional. From Spider Gap descend the north side — about 100 vertical feet of the steepest snow (softer, less sun-affected snow tends to be climber's-left/north), then scree, then an easing snowfield — down roughly 3.5 miles past the Lyman Glacier and Upper Lyman Lakes to Lower Lyman Lake (~5,587 ft). From Lower Lyman Lake, climb back up through open meadows for about 1.8 miles to Cloudy Pass (~6,438 ft), the normal camp/staging point for the peak. From Cloudy Pass, Cloudy Peak's summit is well under a mile away and about 1,500 ft higher: an obvious boot path leads up through wildflower meadows onto rocky talus, gaining the peak's southwest ridge. Follow the ridge crest itself — straying off it onto the flanking slopes drops you into seriously unstable scree/talus — picking a careful line through loose talus blocks to avoid kicking rock onto anyone below; the ridge has real exposure with a precipitous drop on its far (north) side. At the base of the final summit block, traverse around to its east side and then work around toward the north (back) side to find a walkable weakness through the Class 4+ short scramble to the true summit; this last bit is narrow with real exposure and is the route's technical crux. Three approaches reach Cloudy Pass: besides the line described here, Cloudy Pass/Cloudy Peak can also be reached via the Buck Creek Trail #1513 from the Trinity Trailhead over Buck Creek Pass, or via the Railroad Creek Trail from Holden Village (reached by Lake Chelan boat/vehicle shuttle) past Lower Lyman Lake — both longer, multi-day alternatives to the Phelps Creek/Spider Gap line described above, which is the one matching the round-trip distance (~39.6 km) and the Leavenworth/US-2 road drive.

gear: harness and 30m rope for the glacier crossing and optional rappel of the class 4 step
light rack (slings, a few small cams/nuts) for the exposed step
before.detailed_rack: Most parties climb this as an unroped scramble, carrying an ice axe and crampons for the snowfield below the ridge. A light rack (a few slings, a 30m rope) is worth having for the short, exposed class 4 moves near the summit notches, where some parties prefer to belay or rappel rather than solo them.
before.rope_note: Rope up for the glacier. The Southeast Glacier remnant is small and its crevasses are usually minor, but crossing it is the one place on this route where the rope is not optional, so carry a harness and a 30 m rope alongside the ice axe and crampons. Above it most parties scramble the Class 3 ground unroped, but there is a short, exposed and insecure Class 4 step near the summit ridge: a few slings and a small cam or nut let you belay or rappel that rather than solo it, and some parties carry a short hand line for one airy notch. Keep the rope out on the way down - the steep snowfield below the notch is worth a belay if it has gone hard, and the glacier is crossed roped again on the way out.
rack: 30m rope for the crossing and optional rappel
A few slings + small cams/nuts for the exposed class 4 step (optional)

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach_variants.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large TAILINGS PILE around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its WEST side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: Several notches in the spur ridge, most of them Class 5 from below — picking the wrong one is the route's real crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier remnant, worst late summer
A short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge with no fixed protection
Standing dead timber and loose footing in the burn above the tailings pile
Two creek crossings that both run high in early-season melt, one of them dependent on a footbridge that may be out
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A NOTCH, AND IT IS THE BEST NEGATIVE MARKER ON THIS PEAK: SEVERAL NOTCHES CUT THE SPUR RIDGE AND MOST OF THEM ARE CLASS 5 FROM BELOW. The one you want is THE HIGHEST NOTCH YOU CAN REACH EASILY, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's RIGHT — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. THE STREAM IS THE HANDRAIL FROM CAMP: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the OUTLET STREAM that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. WHAT HAPPENS IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE NOTCH, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn LEFT and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. THE LAST OBSTACLE IS ONE MOVE, NOT A PITCH. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A NOTE ON THE ROUTE'S NAME: this route is listed as the South Route with a south-east aspect, and everything published about it describes the EAST-facing glacier remnant and the upper NORTH-EAST ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

weather.typical: Drier east-side (rain-shadow) climate than the west-slope Cascades, but still cold and snowy at elevation; most stable in midsummer

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Loose talus and rockfall are the primary consequence-of-a-slip concerns; the long, committing approach through the Entiat/Railroad Creek drainage means any injury is remote self-rescue terrain with slow evacuation

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer/fall scramble route; not covered by any of NWAC's 10 forecast zones

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard: the route crosses the (much-diminished but present) Southeast Glacier remnant on both approach and descent — rope up for glacier travel, especially early in the season, as crevasses are documented on this crossing.

obj_haz: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard typical of North Cascades glaciers
Loose/exposed rock in the class 4-5 summit scrambling
Very remote, infrequently-traveled terrain with limited route-finding beta
No road access — long approach via boat and trail

before.best_season: Trip reports and guide sources point to a core early-to-mid-summer window (roughly June into August) as the sweet spot: seasonal snow still eases travel in the upper basin and on the steep slopes below Dark Fin Col, and the Dark Glacier's crevasses tend to be more consistently snow-bridged, giving firmer "styrofoam" snow conditions with comparatively low crevasse danger. By late summer and fall (August-October) more crevasses are exposed and the glacier becomes less stable, while earlier in spring the approach and glacier remain fully snow-covered. Dark Peak is broadly reckoned reasonably climbable May through October.

access.fees: No fee for wilderness travel or camping itself; the Stehekin Valley shuttle bus fare is roughly $10/adult each way, and the Lake Chelan ferry/floatplane fare is separate and not free
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) — same Glacier Peak Wilderness system that covers Glacier Peak itself (one contiguous wilderness spanning both Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forests).
access.permit: A free NPS backcountry/wilderness camping permit is required for designated campsites along the Agnes Creek corridor (Fivemile Camp, Swamp Creek Camp); permits have historically been issued in Stehekin at the Golden West Visitor Center, which has had reduced/no seasonal ranger staffing in recent years -- confirm the current permit process with North Cascades National Park before the trip
access.closures: Stehekin Valley Road and area trails sustained significant damage from December 2025 atmospheric-river flooding and debris flows; an interim elevated road section (Company Creek Road) was completed by June 2026, but NPS trail crews were still reconstructing damaged trails park-wide as of mid-2026 -- check the park's Trail Conditions page and Stehekin flood-update page before attempting this route
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) on the peak and upper basin/glacier; the High Bridge/Agnes Creek Trail approach corridor lies within the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, North Cascades National Park Service Complex
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chiwawa/Entiat Ranger Districts) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at some trailheads (fee day-use sites) — $5/day or $30/year.
